JSON: Name: interacting_filament_vesicle_morphogenesis Title: Combined theoretical modeling and molecular-dynamics investigation of how long-range interfilament interactions control vesicle morphogenesis Short Hypothesis: Increasing the strength of long-range repulsive interactions between two enclosed filament loops causes reproducible, parameter-dependent morphological transitions of the confining vesicle (axisymmetric convex → concave → asymmetric/necked → elongated/rod-like), with transition thresholds monotonically decreasing with increased filament length and increasing with filament bending stiffness. Related Work: Prior approaches have characterized membrane–filament couplings in three partially overlapping directions: (1) continuum energy-minimization and spherical-harmonics parameterizations of vesicle shapes with constrained inclusions or single filaments, (2) coarse-grained simulations and in vitro reconstitutions of active cytoskeletal networks inside vesicles (actomyosin, microtubule–motor systems) exploring dynamic shape fluctuations and active deformation, and (3) mechanics of filament packing and buckling under purely geometric confinement. Limitations across these approaches include: most continuum and numerical studies focus on single open or closed filaments and do not include tunable long-range nonlocal filament–filament repulsion; reconstitution and active-filament simulations emphasize internally generated stresses rather than systematic control of interaction range/strength or electrostatic-like repulsion; and existing packing studies lack coupling to a deformable Helfrich membrane with full phase-diagram mapping. Additionally, prior computational work either uses static energy minimization without validating with particle-based dynamics or uses dynamics without exhaustive parameter sweeps linking filament stiffness, length, interaction range, and membrane tension. The unresolved gap is a unified, quantitative mapping from filament mechanical properties and long-range interfilament interaction parameters to vesicle morphology and transition thresholds under both isotropic (Δp=0) and fixed reduced-volume confinement. Abstract: We address the mechanistic role of long-range interfilament interactions in shaping lipid vesicles containing closed filament loops. We combine continuum energy minimization (spherical-harmonic vesicle parameterization with constrained charged filaments) and coarse-grained molecular-dynamics simulations to map morphological phase behavior as a function of filament bending stiffness, filament length, and nonlocal interaction strength. The primary contribution is a set of quantitative phase diagrams and energy- and tension-resolved pathways that identify when interfilament repulsion dominates total system energy and triggers discontinuous and continuous morphological transitions (convex→concave→necked→elongated). We further characterize the effects of ionic screening, inhomogeneous filament segments, and magnetic-dipole-based repulsion as alternative interaction mechanisms. Expected outcomes include reproducible threshold relations between interaction strength, length, stiffness and morphology; mechanistic markers (membrane tension jumps, filament bending energy changes) diagnostic of transitions; and practical design rules for synthetic vesicle systems where filament interactions are used to control shape. These results provide a testable, predictive foundation for experimental realization of filament-mediated vesicle morphogenesis. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Numerical-optimization dataset: grid of parameter triples {YI/(κR) ∈ {0.1, 1, 10}, L/(πR) ∈ [1.0, 3.0] sampled at 0.1 increments, χ ∈ [0, 40] sampled at 0.5 increments} under two confinement conditions: Δp=0 and fixed reduced volume v ∈ {0.9, 0.7}. (2) MD simulation dataset: corresponding subset of 120 representative parameter points sampled to capture phase boundaries (e.g., around predicted transitions), each with 5 independent random seeds. Baselines: (A) filament-free vesicle (membrane only), (B) two filaments with interfilament interaction disabled (χ=0), (C) single filament of equal total length, (D) energy-minimization-only predictions vs MD validation, (E) screened Coulomb cases with Debye lengths λD ∈ {10, 1, 0.1} (dimensionless units), and (F) dipole–dipole (magnetic) interaction substitution. Evaluation metrics: morphological classification label (discrete: D∞h, D2, C2h, Ci, etc.), continuous shape descriptors: asphericity, reduced volume, neck radius, principal axis aspect ratio, spherical-harmonic coefficient spectrum (l up to 20), membrane bending energy (Em), filament bending energy (Ef), intrafilament and interfilament interaction energies (Eintra, Einter), membrane tension σ (= −∂Etot/∂A numerically estimated), and time-series of these quantities for MD. Experimental setup – numerical optimization: spherical-harmonic parameterization up to lmax=20, constrained nonlinear optimization (sequential quadratic programming) enforcing area and filament length constraints; energy terms: Helfrich membrane bending, worm-like-chain filament bending, regularized Coulomb inter/intrafilament energies with mollifier M; output optimized shapes and energies. Experimental setup – MD: coarse-grained one-particle-thick lipid membrane model, filaments as bead-spring chains with harmonic angle potentials; electrostatics solved with P3M; LAMMPS implementation; thermostat: Langevin, temperature kBT=1, timestep Δt=0.005 (reduced units); equilibration 5×10^6 steps, production sampling 5×10^6 steps; box size adjusted per morphology; 5 independent seeds per parameter point. Ablations and comparisons: (i) Disable interfilament term to measure morphological baseline; (ii) vary χ while holding YI and L fixed to map σ–χ curves and detect discontinuities; (iii) vary filament stiffness holding others fixed to quantify threshold shifts; (iv) compare unscreened Coulomb vs screened Coulomb (λD sweep); (v) replace Coulomb with dipole–dipole interaction to test alternative physical realization. Analysis: detect transition lines from discontinuities or kinks in Etot, σ, Ef and from sudden changes in discrete morphology label; compute phase diagrams; statistical significance by bootstrapping over seeds (95% CI for transition χ at each grid point). Risk Factors and Limitations: Modeling assumptions and mapping: the continuum Coulomb-like interaction is an abstraction and may not quantitatively map to experimental electrostatic or magnetic interactions; discretization of charges and finite MD box/periodic boundary effects (finite-size artifacts) can bias effective χ and energy estimates. Parameter sensitivity and initial-condition dependence: energy minima and MD outcomes may depend on initial filament placement and numerical resolution; multiple local minima may complicate phase-boundary identification. Computational cost and scalability: exhaustive high-resolution parameter sweeps with MD are expensive (multi-million-timestep runs multiplied by seeds); exploration of larger filament numbers or very long filaments may be infeasible. Biological relevance and generalization: results obtained for two identical closed loops and coarse-grained membranes may not generalize to dense cytoskeletal networks, open filaments, or membranes with embedded proteins/lipid heterogeneity. Screening and environment dependence: strong ionic screening (small Debye length) can suppress the predicted morphologies, requiring higher interaction strengths that may be experimentally unrealistic. Experimental feasibility: realizing tunable, uniformly charged closed filament loops with controllable long-range repulsion and prescribed stiffness/length in vitro may be technically challenging. Measurement and classification limits: discrete morphology labels depend on chosen order parameters and thresholds; ambiguous intermediate states may be misclassified.
